# A faster matrix multiplication algorithm through structured optimization

**Abstract**

We present a new asymptotic matrix multiplication construction yielding \(\omega<2.37115924\), and therefore an algorithm that multiplies two \(n\times n\) matrices in _O(n_<sup>2.37115924</sup>) arithmetic operations over the rationals, reals, or complex numbers. The construction improves the bound 2.371177 of Dupont et al. within the combination-loss framework for the Coppersmith–Winograd tensor. Our approach combines a shared recursive parameter family with a conditioned optimization procedure that addresses two obstacles: weak gradients at low-mass constituents and competing bottlenecks in the retained exponent. A mass- and probability-dependent rescaling supports quasi-Newton optimization in 212820 coordinates, while a six-control correction balances the three extraction roles at each relevant stage. Positive rational entropy-dual factors and an independent ordinary-string verifier turn the resulting construction into an exact certificate. The verified upper-bound expression lies in [2.3711592385931075066123, 2.3711592385931075066124]. The complete witness and an offline verifier using only the Python standard library accompany the paper.

### 1 Introduction

We give a new asymptotic algorithm for matrix multiplication, reducing the exponent bound to 2.37115924. The improvement arises from a specific recursive tensor construction discovered by an optimization procedure tailored to the geometry and bottlenecks of combination-loss analysis. The resulting rational construction is accompanied by an independently implemented exact verifier.

The matrix multiplication exponent \(\omega_\mathbb{Q}\) is the infimum of the real numbers _a_ such that two \(n\times n\) matrices over Q can be multiplied using \(O(n^{a+\varepsilon})\) arithmetic operations for every \(\varepsilon>0\). We write \(\omega=\omega_\mathbb{Q}\) throughout. Since Strassen’s subcubic algorithm [15], successive improvements have relied on algebraic constructions that reduce many matrix products to tensor decompositions. The Coppersmith–Winograd tensor [7], together with the asymptotic sum inequality [13], provides the starting point for the construction studied here.

Combination-loss analysis refines the laser method by retaining additional combinations of tensor constituents. Its recent developments include asymmetric hashing [8], refined bounds for square and rectangular multiplication [18], and the asymmetric framework of Alman et al. [2]. These theorems reduce an upper-bound calculation to a constrained optimization problem involving probability distributions, entropy penalties, and recursively derived matrix dimensions. A feasible parameter choice is sufficient; global optimality is unnecessary.

Dupont et al. [9] formulate this optimization at recursion level four and obtain \(\omega<2.371177\). The central question addressed here is how to obtain a better algorithmic construction from that

<tbc>framework. We combine parameter sharing with mass-dependent conditioning and explicit correction of the extraction bottlenecks. The resulting construction proves the following algorithmic guarantee.

**Theorem 1.** _There is an algorithm for multiplying two_ \(n\times n\) _matrices over_ Q _using O(n_<sup>2.37115924</sup>) _arithmetic operations. More precisely, the square matrix multiplication exponent satisfies_

\(\omega_\mathbb{Q}<2.37115924.\)

_The same algorithmic guarantee holds over every characteristic-zero extension of_ Q_, including_ R _and_ C.

Relative to the bound of Dupont et al., the reduction in the exponent is \(1.776\cdot 10^{-5}\). This is an improvement in the polynomial growth rate of the arithmetic complexity: the corresponding leading powers of _n_ differ by a factor _n_<sup>0.00001776</sup>. As with other algorithms obtained through this tensor framework, the guarantee is asymptotic; the exponent alone does not specify a practical crossover size. A contemporaneous public computational release \[4\] reports an upper-bound expression approximately equal to 2.371169352063661; the present certified expression is also smaller than that value.

1 places the result among selected major improvements in the matrix multiplication exponent.

1: Selected improvements in upper bounds on the matrix multiplication exponent. Years refer to the cited publications; some results appeared earlier in proceedings or preprints. The Vassilevska Williams entry uses a bound from the corrected full version. The BSD row is a public computational certificate, rather than a paper, and its bound is rounded upward from the exact rational certificate.

1. **A faster asymptotic algorithm from a compact construction.** The rational witness specifies an instance of the level-four combination-loss construction with _q_=5. Shared descendant parameters and binary-tree position symmetries give a 212820-coordinate family in which the improved exponent is attained. Unfolding the shared graph preserves admissibility, and six global coordinate permutations produce equal final matrix dimensions.<tbc>

2. **Conditioning adapted to constituent masses.** We rescale each numerical coordinate using its occurrence mass and local probability, including marginal-variance weights for entropy-dual coordinates. This addresses the disparate gradient scales of the recursive construction. The rescaling is refreshed between limited-memory quasi-Newton solves, with a larger scale range for low-mass constituents.<tbc>

3. **A six-control correction for extraction bottlenecks.** The root and two constituent stages each contribute a minimum of three role totals. We couple an augmented-Lagrangian continuation to a separate correction using two controls per stage. A \(6\times 6\) Newton system targets the six role differences, and candidate selection uses the original minimum-based objective. This focuses the correction on the bottlenecks that directly determine the exponent.<tbc>

4. **An exact, independently checkable construction.** The export preserves positive entropy- dual factors as arbitrary-size rational numbers. An independent verifier expands ordinary ternary strings and assembles all physical-coordinate contributions before applying the published minima. The resulting finite certificate can be checked offline, separately from the optimization implementation.

These contributions build on the tensor theorem of Alman et al. and the optimization formulation of Dupont et al. The orbit representation and equality-constrained approach were informed by computational notes shared by Eric Naslund. Softmax parameterization, quasi-Newton optimization, augmented Lagrangians, entropy duality, and rational interval arithmetic are established tools; the methodological contribution is their specified adaptation and integration for the construction certified here.

Section 2 specifies the construction and the restricted parameter family. Section 3 describes the numerical continuation and rational export. Section 4 gives the certificate and the proof of Theorem 1. The appendix supplies implementation-level lemmas for shared parameters and logarithm enclosures.

## 2 Construction and parameter family

The construction is an instance of the combination-loss framework of [2], in the formulation of [9, Section 2]. The new algorithm is specified by a rational recursive extraction construction within that framework. Its parameters determine the retained matrix products and their asymptotic dimensions. We use the Coppersmith–Winograd tensor with parameter _q_=5 and recursion level \(\ell^*=4\). Thus the starting tensor is \(\mathrm{CW}_5^{\otimes 8}\), whose asymptotic rank cost, in binary logarithms, is

\(C=2^{\ell^*-1}\mathrm{log}_2(q+2)=8\mathrm{log}_27.\) (1)

Below we specify the restricted family used in the numerical search. All restrictions are parameter identifications or symmetries allowed by the published construction.

## 2.1 Shapes, complete split distributions, and recursive parameters

A level-\(\ell\) shape is a triple _s_=(_i,j,k_) of nonnegative integers with \(i+j+k=2^\ell\). For each coordinate \(w\in\{X,Y,Z\}\), its complete split distribution \(\beta_s^w\) is supported on

\(\mathcal{S}_{\ell,s_w}=\left\{L\in\{0,1,2\}^{2^{\ell-1}}:\sum_tL_t=s_w\right\}.\)

Different occurrences of the same shape may have different parameters; we suppress the occurrence index when it is unambiguous. The root distribution \(\alpha^*\) is supported on all 153 shapes of level 4.

For a positive shape _s_ at level \(\ell\ge 3\), define its allowed half-shapes by

\(D_s=\{u\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}^3:u_X+u_Y+u_Z=2^{\ell-1},u_w\le s_w\text{for all}w\}.\)

There are six extraction regions, indexed by permutations \(p_r:\{X,Y,Z\}\rightarrow\{X,Y,Z\}\). At an occurrence _v_ of shape _s_, the parameters comprise a probability vector \((A_{v,r})_{r=1}^6\), a distribution \(\alpha_{v,r}\) on _D<sub>s</sub>_ for each region, and references _c(v,r,u_) to children of shape _u_. The regional complete split distributions are

\(B_{v,r}^w=\sum_{u\in D_s}\alpha_{v,r}(u)\big(\beta_{c(v,r,u)}^w\otimes\beta_{c(v,r,s-u)}^w\big),\beta_v^w=\sum_{r=1}^6A_{v,r}B_{v,r}^w,\) (2)

where the tensor product denotes ordered concatenation of the two split strings. In the family used for the final witness,

\(\alpha_{v,r}(u)=\alpha_{v,r}(s-u).\) (3)

The root distribution \(\alpha^*\) has no corresponding constraint under permutation of its three coordinates.

For a shape with a zero coordinate, one nonzero coordinate’s complete split distribution is free. The other is its image under \(L\mapsto\mathbf{2}-L\), and the zero coordinate is concentrated on the all-zero string. A positive shape at level 2 is a permutation of (1,1,2). It has a parameter \(\mu\in[0,1/2]\): each coordinate of value 1 has probabilities (1/2,1/2) on (01,10), and the coordinate of value 2 has probabilities \((\mu,1-2\mu,\mu)\) on (02,11,20).

The search imposes two further identifications. First, complete split distributions are invariant under the group generated by exchanging the two children of each node in a complete binary tree on the string positions. Only one probability per orbit is stored, with the orbit multiplicity included in normalization and entropy evaluation. Equation (3) makes the recursive product construction compatible with exchanging the two halves. Second, at the transition from level 4 to level 3, children with the same parent occurrence and the same half-shape are shared across the six regions. At the transition from level 3 to level 2, children are indexed separately by parent, region, and half-shape. These choices give 153, 1785, and 41310 stored occurrences at levels 4, 3, and 2, respectively. Unfolding the shared references produces an admissible recursive construction; reuse of a parameter does not identify tensor variables between distinct occurrences.

Including distribution logits, leaf parameters, region logits, and entropy-dual parameters, the search has 212820 real coordinates. This is a coordinate count, not the dimension of the feasible set: softmax gauge freedoms and the paired representation in (3) introduce redundancies. The final witness is expanded into ordinary ordered ternary strings, so its verification does not rely on the orbit representation.

## 2.2 Certified entropy penalties

The maximum-entropy penalties can be bounded without certifying the solution of an auxiliary optimization problem. Let \(\alpha\) be a distribution on an allowed set of shapes _D_, and let \(H_D^\mathrm{max}(\alpha)\) be the maximum entropy of a distribution on _D_ having the same three marginals as \(\alpha\). Choose arbitrary strictly positive factors _f<sub>X</sub>,f<sub>Y</sub>,f<sub>Z</sub>_, and put

\(t_u=\prod_{w\in\{X,Y,Z\}}f_w(u_w),U_D(\alpha;f)=\mathrm{log}_2\left(\sum_{u\in D}t_u\right)-\sum_{u\in D}\alpha(u)\mathrm{log}_2t_u.\) (4)

Then \(H_D^\mathrm{max}(\alpha)\le U_D(\alpha;f)\). Indeed, if \(\rho\) has the prescribed marginals, then

\(\sum_u\rho(u)\mathrm{log}_2t_u=\sum_u\alpha(u)\mathrm{log}_2t_u.\)

Nonnegativity of the relative entropy of \(\rho\) with respect to the distribution \(t/\sum_ut_u\) proves the inequality. Therefore

\(\widehat{P}_D(\alpha;f)=U_D(\alpha;f)-H(\alpha)\) (5)

is a valid upper bound on the combination-loss penalty. Its use can only reduce the retained exponent supplied by the construction. The factors are optimized along with the other parameters, but their optimality is not required for the certificate.

For completeness, the local quantities evaluated by the implementation can be written as follows. Extend the notation _H_ to a nonnegative vector by \(H(v)=-\sum_tv_t\mathrm{log}_2v_t\), with 0log<sub>2</sub>0=0. For child weights _a<sub>u</sub>_, distributions \(\beta_u^w\), and a set _S_ of exceptional child shapes, define

\(\eta_w(a,\beta;S)=\sum_{u\in S}a_uH(\beta_u^w)+\sum_t\left[H(v_t)-H\left(\left[\sum_Lv_t(L)\right]\right)\right],v_t=\sum_{u\notin Su_w=t}a_u\beta_u^w.\) (6)

Here _H_([_b_])=-_b_log<sub>2</sub>_b_; hence each bracket in (6) is the mass of _v<sub>t</sub>_ times the entropy of its normalization. At a positive occurrence _v_ in region _r_, write (_x,y,z_)=(_p<sub>r</sub>(X),p<sub>r</sub>(Y),p<sub>r</sub>(Z_)) and \(a_u=\alpha_{v,r}(u)+\alpha_{v,r}(s-u)\). The three local retained quantities are

\(c_{v,r,X}=H((\alpha_{v,r})_x)-\widehat{P}_{D_s}(\alpha_{v,r};f_{v,r}),c_{v,r,Y}=H(B_{v,r}^y)-\eta_y(a,\beta;\{u:u_z=0\}),c_{v,r,Z}=H(B_{v,r}^z)-\eta_z(a,\beta;\{u:u_x=0\text{or}u_y=0\}).\) (7)

The subscripts _X,Y,Z_ on _c_ denote extraction roles, rather than physical coordinates.

Let _m<sub>v</sub>_ be the mass of an occurrence. Root occurrences have mass \(m_v=\alpha^*(s_v)\), and masses are propagated by

\(m_{c(v,r,u)}+=m_vA_{v,r}\big(\alpha_{v,r}(u)+\alpha_{v,r}(s_v-u)\big).\) (8)

Contributions from all references to a shared child are added. The stage role totals are

\(R_{\ell,k}=\sum_{v\text{positive at level}\ell} m_v\sum_{r=1}^6A_{v,r}c_{v,r,k},\ell\in\{4,3\},k\in\{X,Y,Z\}.\) (9)

At the canonical root, use _D_={_s:s<sub>X</sub>+s<sub>Y</sub>+s<sub>Z</sub>_=16} in (5). If \(\overline{\beta^w}=\sum_s\alpha^*(s)\beta_s^w\), the analogous root totals are

\(R_{0,X}=H(\alpha_X^*)-\widehat{P}_D(\alpha^*;f^*),R_{0,Y}=H(\overline{\beta^Y})-\eta_Y(\alpha^*,\beta;\{s:s_Z=0\}),R_{0,Z}=H(\overline{\beta^Z})-\eta_Z(\alpha^*,\beta;\{s:s_X=0\text{or}s_Y=0\}).\text{(10)}\)

## 2.3 Six-copy symmetrization and the exponent objective

The complete construction consists of six globally coordinate-permuted copies of the canonical parameter tree, each assigned weight 1/6. This symmetrization is performed in addition to the six local extraction regions. We write \(\widehat{E}\) for the conservative retained exponent obtained after inserting the entropy upper bounds (4); it need not equal the exponent obtained with exact maximum-entropy penalties. The six-copy symmetry yields the following exact reduction of the stage formula for this \(\widehat{E}\):

\(\widehat{E}=min_kR_{0,k}+min_kR_{4,k}+min_kR_{3,k}+E_2.\) (11)

To see why the minima have this form, let _K<sub>r,w</sub>_ be the canonical contribution in physical coordinate _w_ from local region _r_, including all occurrence masses and region weights. For a fixed physical orientation _h_ and a local permutation _p<sub>r</sub>_, precisely one global copy contributes, namely \(g=h\circ p_r^{-1}\). Its contribution in physical coordinate _h(k_) is _K<sub>r,p<sub>r</sub>(k_)</sub>/6. Thus the three totals at orientation _h_ are \(R_{\ell,k}/6\), and summing the minimum over the six physical orientations gives \(min_kR_{\ell,k}\). This argument uses the particular six-copy symmetry; it does not interchange a minimum and a sum for arbitrary inputs.

The same symmetry makes the three terminal dimension exponents equal. The contribution of a positive level-2 occurrence with parameter \(\mu_v\) is

\(E_{2,v}=\frac{m_v}{3}\big(2+H(\mu_v,1-2\mu_v,\mu_v)\big),M_v=\frac{m_v}{3}(2-2\mu_v)log_2q.\) (12)

A zero-coordinate occurrence contributes no term to _E_<sub>2</sub> and contributes

\(M_v=\frac{m_v}{3}\left(H(\beta_v^w)+\sum_L\beta_v^w(L)\#_1(L)log_2q\right)\) (13)

to _M_, where _w_ is any nonzero coordinate and #<sub>1</sub>(_L_) counts the entries equal to 1. Complementation shows that either nonzero coordinate gives the same expression. If two coordinates vanish, all distributions are point masses and the matrix-size contribution is zero. Summing these terms gives _E_<sub>2</sub> and the common matrix-size exponent _M\>_0.

The degeneration theorem and asymptotic sum inequality imply

\(\omega\le\widehat{\Omega}(x):=\frac{C-\widehat{E}(x)}{M(x)}.\) (14)

Equivalently, to prove \(\omega<\tau\), it suffices to exhibit admissible parameters for which

\(\widehat{E}(x)+\tau M(x)-C>0.\) (15)

All three minima in (11) are retained in the certified evaluation.

### 2.4 From the construction to a multiplication algorithm

The rational parameter assignment specifies the retained constituents, their multiplicities, and their matrix dimensions in the published tensor construction. For increasing tensor powers, the extraction theorem yields independent matrix multiplication tensors with normalized logarithmic multiplicity at least \(\widehat{E}\), common normalized logarithmic dimension _M_, and input rank cost at most _C_, up to vanishing losses in the normalized exponents. The six global coordinate permutations balance the final dimensions. The asymptotic sum inequality then gives \(\omega\le\widehat{\Omega}=(C-\widehat{E})/M\).

For every \(\varepsilon>0\), the standard conversion from these tensor bounds to algorithms yields multiplication of two \(n\times n\) matrices in \(O(n^{\widehat{\Omega}+\varepsilon})\) arithmetic operations. The rational parameters are a concrete admissible input to the degeneration and recursive blocking machinery of \[2, 13\]; the entropy-dual factors certify the analysis of the retained constituents.

Since the exact certificate proves \(\widehat{\Omega}<2.37115924\), choose \(0<\varepsilon<2.37115924-\widehat{\Omega}\). This yields the _O(n_<sup>2.37115924</sup>) algorithm stated in Theorem 1. The improvement is carried by the new recursive extraction parameters and their certified analysis. The conversion from that construction to a matrix multiplication algorithm uses the established tensor framework.

## 3 Structured optimization of the construction

The optimization procedure is organized around three structural features of the construction: occurrence masses span different scales, the retained exponent is governed by competing role minima, and the final parameters must admit rigorous certification. We address these with coordinate conditioning, a separate bottleneck correction, and positive rational export. The orbit representation and equality-constrained starting approach were informed by computational notes shared by Eric Naslund; the following sections specify the implementation used here. The documented procedure differs from the Adam and differentiated Sinkhorn approach described in \[9, Section 3\] by combining conditioned quasi-Newton solves with a separate six-control correction.

### 3.1 Smooth parameterization and balanced search objective

Probability vectors are represented by softmax logits. For a local split distribution, a raw logit _z<sub>u</sub>_ is replaced by (_z<sub>u</sub>+z_<sub>_s-u_</sub>)/2 before applying the softmax, imposing (3). For an orbit of size _b_, adding ln_b_ before normalization converts a per-string logit into an orbit mass. Leaf parameters use \(\mu=\frac{1}{2}\mathrm{sigmoid}(z)\). Entropy-dual factors are represented by unconstrained logarithms. These transformations enforce the local probability constraints during optimization, while the exported witness enforces them exactly.

Near the selected point, the three roles are nearly tied at the root and at each constituent stage. We exploit this structure in the numerical search by defining, for \(t\in\{0,4,3\}\),<tbc>

\(\overline{R_t}=\frac{1}{3}\sum_kR_{t,k},h_{t,Y}=R_{t,Y}-R_{t,X},h_{t,Z}=R_{t,Z}-R_{t,X}.\)

<tbc>The six quantities _h_ are equality residuals. The difference between the average-based retained exponent and the actual one is exactly

\(\mathcal{B}(x)=\sum_{t\in\{0,4,3\}}\left(\overline{R_t}(x)-\mathrm{min}_kR_{t,k}(x)\right)\ge 0.\) (16)

Thus an increase in the average can be lost to greater role imbalance. The condition _h_=0 makes B=0; it identifies the six differences targeted by the correction below. With target parameter<tbc>

\(\tau_0=2.37116\), the augmented-Lagrangian objective minimized during the final continuation is

\(\mathcal{L}(x;\lambda,\rho)=C-E_2(x)-\sum_{t\in\{0,4,3\}}\overline{R_t}(x)-\tau_0M(x)+\langle\lambda,h(x)\rangle+\frac{\rho}{2}\|h(x)\|_2^2.\) (17)

The average-role expression is a search surrogate. It agrees with the retained exponent only when _h_=0; otherwise it can overestimate the retained exponent. No conclusion about \(\omega\) is drawn from this surrogate alone, and equality of the roles is not a hypothesis of the certified construction.

After each outer pass, the multipliers are updated by \(\lambda\leftarrow\lambda+\rho h\). The penalty starts at \(\rho=20\) and is doubled after every fourth pass if \(\|h\|_\infty>2\cdot 10^{-7}\). The final continuation starts from a previously obtained point with minimum-based objective approximately 2.371161129895562, taking multipliers from the preceding continuation and resetting the penalty to 20. It consists of 20 outer passes, each with an inner iteration limit of 500, and records 10087 objective-and-gradient evaluations. The numerical computations use double precision, automatic differentiation in JAX, and SciPy’s L-BFGS-B implementation [5], without explicit bounds on the transformed coordinates.

## 3.2 Mass-dependent conditioning of quasi-Newton steps

The occurrence masses and local probabilities vary substantially in magnitude. The source of the scale mismatch can already be seen in a local term _mg(p_) with softmax probabilities _p_, holding its incoming mass _m_ fixed: its logit gradient is<tbc>

\(\frac{\partial(mg(p))}{\partial z_i}=mp_i\left(\frac{\partial g}{\partial p_i}-\sum_jp_j\frac{\partial g}{\partial p_j}\right).\)

<tbc>Small masses, and often small probabilities, suppress these coordinate gradients. This motivates a diagonal rescaling using mass and probability weights, also suggested by the corresponding Fisher- information scales. At the beginning of an outer pass, let _x_<sup>(0)</sup> be the current parameter vector. Optimize in coordinates _y_ defined by

\(x=x^{(0)}+Sy,S_{ii}=clip_{[0.03,10^6]}\left(max\{w_i,10^{-14}\}^{-1/2}\right).\) (18)

The weight _w<sub>i</sub>_ is the current occurrence mass times the appropriate local probability: orbit mass for a free complete split distribution, region weight for region logits, and region weight times split probability for split logits. Root logits use their root probabilities. For a dual marginal coordinate of marginal probability _p_, the weight is the occurrence and region mass times _p_(1-_p_). A leaf-\(\mu\) logit uses its occurrence mass. This is a diagonal conditioning rule, not an exact natural-gradient method. The scale is held fixed throughout each inner solve and recomputed between outer passes.

Each inner solve uses L-BFGS history length 40, function tolerance 10<sup>-15</sup>, gradient tolerance 10<sup>-9</sup>, and a line-search limit of 35. Relative to the preceding continuation, the scale cap is increased from 10<sup>5</sup> to 10<sup>6</sup>, the mass floor is decreased from 10<sup>-12</sup> to 10<sup>-14</sup>, and the history length is increased from 30 to 40. These changes concern numerical conditioning only; they do not alter the admissible tensor family.

## 3.3 Balancing extraction bottlenecks with six controls

The bottleneck gap in (16) motivates a correction that acts directly on the six role differences, even though the full parameter vector has 212820 coordinates. After every second outer pass, this<tbc>

separate correction attempts to reduce the six role-equality residuals using only six scalar controls. Two controls add to the root logits the features<tbc>

\(\left(\frac{s_X-s_Y}{16},\frac{s_Y-s_Z}{16}\right).\)

<tbc>At each level \(\ell\in\{4,3\}\), two controls add to the region logits at shape _s_ and permutation _p<sub>r</sub>_ the features

\(\left(\frac{s_{p_r(Y)}-s_{p_r(X)}}{2^\ell},\frac{s_{p_r(Z)}-s_{p_r(X)}}{2^\ell}\right).\)

A \(6\times 6\) Jacobian is estimated by central differences with step 10<sup>-4</sup>. Up to four Newton corrections are computed by least squares with relative singular-value cutoff 10<sup>-12</sup>, scaling a correction down if its infinity norm exceeds 1. The balancing attempt terminates early when \(\|h\|_\infty<10^{-11}\).

Both unbalanced iterates and balanced candidates are evaluated using the minimum-based objective (14), and the best candidate is retained. Balancing is a candidate-generation step: the augmented-Lagrangian continuation proceeds from its own iterate. In floating-point monitoring, a minimum of three entries is evaluated with the conservative approximation

\(\mathrm{sin}\mathrm{n}_\varepsilon(a)=-\varepsilon\mathrm{ln}\sum_{k=1}^3e^{-a_k/\varepsilon},\varepsilon=10^{-14},\)

which lies between \(\mathrm{min}_ka_k-\varepsilon\mathrm{ln}3\) and min_<sub>k</sub>a<sub>k</sub>_. The final rational evaluation uses the actual minima.

The selected point comes from the balancing step following the last outer pass. Its floating-point minimum-based objective is approximately 2.3711592385931133. The search is local and supplies no certificate of global optimality. The reported settings describe the continuation that produced the witness; reproduction of the mathematical bound requires the final witness and its checker, independently of repeating the optimization trajectory.

## 3.4 Positive rational export and independent reconstruction

The selected probabilities are converted to integer numerators with denominator 2<sup>80</sup>, preserving normalization and the paired symmetry of local split probabilities. Orbit masses are then expanded into equal probabilities for their ordinary strings. Increasing the common denominator to 2<sup>96</sup> makes this expansion exact, since the relevant orbit sizes are powers of two. Consequently the delivered witness contains rational distributions on explicitly ordered strings rather than an orbit-compressed numerical model.

The logarithmic dual parameters are converted separately. In each factor row, subtract the smallest active logarithmic value before exponentiation and rational approximation. The resulting active factors are at least 1, and their integer numerators are not restricted to machine-word size. This choice preserves large ratios without forcing small factors onto a fixed positive floor. In particular, normalizing by the largest factor and clipping small rounded values could substantially weaken the entropy bound despite preserving positivity. The chosen row normalization avoids that loss. Such row rescalings leave (4) unchanged. More generally, the validity of the bound requires only strict positivity of the exported factors; neither a small approximation error nor a stationarity check is an assumption of the verification.

The checker validates support, nonnegativity, exact normalization, child shapes, complementary references, and the recursively reconstructed complete split distributions. It evaluates the six global copies in physical coordinates before taking the published minima. Binary logarithms and subsequent expressions are enclosed by rational outward intervals. The numerical result is reported in Section 4.

## 4 Rigorous verification

Let _E_pub denote the retained exponent computed with exact maximum-entropy penalties, and let \(\widehat{E}\) denote the value in (11), using the positive-factor bounds (4). Since these bounds only increase the penalties, and all mass weights are nonnegative,

\(\widehat{E}\le E_\mathrm{pub}.\) (19)

Every sum and minimum occurring after the replacement is coordinatewise nondecreasing, which preserves this inequality.

**Proposition 1** (Certificate implication)**.** _For admissible parameters, suppose the six-copy construction gives the conservative retained exponent_ \(\widehat{E}\)_, common matrix-size exponent M\>_0_, and rank exponent C. Then_

\(\omega\le\frac{C-\widehat{E}}{M}.\)

_Consequently, a rational target_ \(\tau\) _satisfying_ \(\widehat{E}+\tau M-C>0\) _proves_ \(\omega<\tau\).

_Proof._ The combination-loss theorem [2], in the formulation of [9, Theorem 1], together with the asymptotic sum inequality [13], gives \(E_\mathrm{pub}+M\omega\le C\). Apply (19), divide by _M\>_0, and rearrange the strict feasibility inequality.

### 4.1 Exact checks and interval evaluation

The witness is a JSON file containing integer numerators for the probabilities and entropy-dual factors, together with node shapes, levels, regional data, and child references. Both declared denominators are 2<sup>96</sup>. The checker reconstructs the distributions on ordinary ordered ternary strings, without importing the optimizer or its orbit representation. ### A.1 Shared recursive parameters

**Lemma 1** (Unfolding shared parameters)**.** _Suppose a finite layered directed acyclic graph specifies the parameters of the combination-loss construction. Assume that every child edge has the prescribed lower level and shape, and that all distributions and leaf parameters satisfy their exact support, normalization, and range conditions. The graph defines an admissible parameter tree by giving each occurrence of a referenced node a separate copy of its parameters and descendants. Its derived distributions and exponent contributions can be evaluated on the graph, accumulating the masses of repeated occurrences before computing contributions linear in those masses._

_Proof._ Unfold the graph recursively. Its levels strictly decrease, so the resulting tree is finite. An induction from the leaves proves that all copies of a graph node have identical complete split distributions: the recursion uses only its parameters and its children’s distributions. Its local entropies and matrix-size coefficients are therefore also identical. Mass propagation, regional sums before minimization, and leaf contributions are linear in the incoming mass. Summing the masses of these copies consequently gives the same result as their separate evaluation. No tensor variables are identified by this parameter sharing.
